title: Kerala (Kochi, Munnar, Alappuzha)
selection: Kerala recorded 0.738 million foreign tourist visits in 2024 (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025, Table 4.1.2), up 13.8% on 2023, and is India's best-known backwater and hill-station destination. Kochi is the main international gateway; Munnar and Alappuzha are the most-visited hill and backwater bases. v2 (2026-11-05): state record rebuilt in the Himachal layout and 16 destinations added, from Kerala Tourism (Department of Tourism) FAQ and destination pages, Incredible India, the Kerala district websites (nic.in / gov.in) and Wikipedia. Where official pages disagree on distances (e.g. Kovalam's airport, 10 vs 15 km), a range is given. The Wayanad district how-to-reach page is placeholder text and is not used; the Pathanamthitta site files Sabarimala and Gavi under each other's URLs. No prices are given.

KS1.claim: Kerala, 38,863 sq km, lies between the Arabian Sea and the Western Ghats, bordered by Karnataka to the north-east and Tamil Nadu to the east.

bound by Karnataka to the northeast, Tamil Nadu to the east, and the Lakshadweep islands in the western vicinity

KS2.claim: Kerala falls into highlands, midlands and a 580 km coastline of beaches and backwaters, threaded by 44 rivers.

evidence.quote: Kerala is divided into three geographical regions: Highlands, which slope down from the Western Ghats onto the Midlands of undulating hills and valleys into an unbroken 580 km long coastline with many picturesque backwaters, interconnected with canals and rivers.
networked by 44 interconnected rivers

KS3.claim: Anamudi, at 2,695 m, is Kerala's highest peak.

evidence.quote: Anamudi, the highest peak in Kerala, rising to 2,695 meters above sea level

evidence.quote: is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala

KS5.claim: Kerala's history turned on the spice trade, which brought Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Chinese, Portuguese, Dutch, French and British traders.

evidence.quote: Celebrated as the Spice Coast of India, ancient Kerala played host to travellers and traders from across the world including the Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Chinese, Portuguese, Dutch, French and the British.

KS6.claim: Kerala has four international airports: Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi, Kozhikode and Kannur.

evidence.quote: easily accessible through its four international airports in Thiruvananthapuram , Kochi , Kozhikode  and Kannur .

KS7.claim: Trains reach most towns except in the hill districts of Idukki and Wayanad; NH 66 runs the length of the coast.

Thiruvananthapuram Central (TVC) is the busiest railway station in the state.

Taxis: Taxis are readily available, especially in major cities.
Renting a car is a great way to explore Kerala at your own pace but driving in Kerala can be challenging.

evidence.quote: the southwest monsoon (Edavappathy) from June to September, the northeast monsoon (Thulavarsham) from October to December, and the summer season from March to May
the winter months (December to February) are mild

the recent years, especially since 2015, have witnessed couple of instances of major flooding, owing to excessive rainfall during the southwest monsoon

on the Pooram day—the day when the moon rises with the Pooram star in the Malayalam Calendar month of Medam

overview.text:
Kerala is a narrow state of 38,863 sq km between the Arabian Sea and the Western Ghats, bordered by Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. It falls into three bands: the forested highlands of the Ghats, rising to Anamudi at 2,695 m; the midlands of hills and plantations; and a 580 km coast of beaches and backwaters, fed by 44 rivers. Thiruvananthapuram is the capital, Kochi the main gateway, and Malayalam the language, with English widely spoken where visitors go.

For centuries this was the Spice Coast, trading pepper and cardamom with Romans, Arabs, Chinese and then the Portuguese, Dutch and British — the reason for Kochi's churches, synagogue and fishing nets. The backwaters, threaded with more than 900 km of waterways, are best seen from a houseboat, a converted rice barge; behind them lie the tea hills of Munnar and the forests of Thekkady and Wayanad.

Kerala's culture is a draw in itself: Kathakali dance-drama, Theyyam in the north, the martial art Kalaripayattu, Ayurveda, snake-boat races and festivals such as Onam and Thrissur Pooram. The food — appam and stew, fish curry in coconut milk, the banana-leaf sadya, Malabar biryani — is reason enough to come. Kerala recorded 22.25 million domestic and 0.738 million foreign tourist visits in 2024.

items.title: Thiruvananthapuram and the south coast
items.body: The capital and its Padmanabhaswamy Temple, the beaches of Kovalam and Varkala's cliffs, Poovar's estuary, and Ponmudi and Neyyar in the hills.

items.title: The backwaters: Alappuzha and Kumarakom

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Kerala has four international airports — Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi, Kozhikode and Kannur. Kochi is the usual gateway for Munnar, Alappuzha and Thekkady; Thiruvananthapuram for Kovalam and Varkala; Kozhikode for Wayanad; Kannur and Mangaluru for the far north.

By rail: trains run along the coast and reach most towns, but not the hill districts of Idukki and Wayanad. Thiruvananthapuram Central is the busiest station; Ernakulam Junction serves Kochi. For Munnar and Thekkady you take the train to Ernakulam, Aluva or Kottayam and continue by road.

By road: NH 66 runs the length of the coast. State and private buses are cheap and go almost everywhere, and taxis are easy to find in the cities; driving yourself is possible but can be challenging. Distances look short but hill roads are slow — Kochi to Munnar takes about 4.5 hours, and Munnar to Thekkady about 4.

best_time.text:
November–February: the peak season, with pleasant weather on the coast and cool days in Munnar and Thekkady. October–February is the best time for a houseboat.

March–May: summer. The coast and midlands are hot and humid (up to about 36°C), but the hill stations stay comfortable.

June–September: the south-west monsoon brings heavy rain and green landscapes. It is a favoured season for Ayurveda, but backwater cruising is suspended at Kumarakom, some Wayanad areas may close, and since 2015 heavy rain has caused major floods more than once. Onam and its boat races fall in August–September.

October–December: the north-east monsoon brings lighter rain, and the Theyyam season in the north begins in December.

where_to_stay.text: Fort Kochi, with heritage hotels and homestays among its colonial streets, is the easiest first night. In the backwaters, spend a night on a houseboat — the state grades them platinum, gold and silver — or stay by the lake at Kumarakom. In the hills, Munnar has hotels and estate stays, and Kumily, by the Periyar reserve, has affordable rooms. On the south coast, Kovalam has everything from five-star hotels to budget cottages and Ayurvedic resorts, while Varkala, on its cliffs, is quieter. Family-run homestays are found across the state; Kerala Tourism lists the government-approved ones.

items.body: Kerala is generally safe, but stay aware of your surroundings.

items.title: When is the best time to visit Kerala?
items.body: November to February for most of the state; October to February for houseboats; the hill stations are pleasant from November to February. June to September is the heavy south-west monsoon.

items.title: Can I take a houseboat in the monsoon?
items.body: In Kumarakom, backwater cruising is not allowed during the south-west monsoon (June–August). October to February is the best season.

items.title: Which airport should I fly into?
items.body: Kochi for Munnar, Alappuzha and Thekkady; Thiruvananthapuram for Kovalam and Varkala; Kozhikode for Wayanad; Kannur for the north.

items.title: Is there a train to Munnar or Wayanad?
items.body: No. The hill districts of Idukki and Wayanad have no railway; take a train to Ernakulam, Aluva or Kottayam for Munnar and Thekkady, or Kozhikode for Wayanad, and continue by road.

items.title: Will I see a tiger in Periyar?
items.body: Probably not — the forest is dense and tiger sightings are highly unlikely. The boat on Periyar Lake is the best chance of seeing elephants, bison and otters.

items.title: When can I see Theyyam?
items.body: The Theyyam season in northern Kerala runs from December to March, mostly in Kannur and Kasaragod.

items.title: Is English spoken?
items.body: Yes, widely in tourist areas. Malayalam is the state language.

overview.text:
Kochi has been a port since at least the 14th century, when ships from across Asia and Europe came for its spices; it is still called the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'. The Portuguese arrived in 1500, the Dutch in 1663 and the British in the 18th century, and each left its mark.

The city is spread out. Fort Kochi and Mattancherry, on the peninsula, hold the history: Chinese fishing nets on the shore, St Francis Church, colonial streets full of galleries, and the palace and synagogue of Mattancherry. Ernakulam, across the water, is the modern city with the stations and hotels. India's first water metro links the mainland with the islands.

Kochi is the usual gateway to Munnar and the backwaters, and October to March is the most pleasant time to visit.

best_time.text: October to March has the most pleasant weather for exploring Kochi. December is busy: the ten-day Cochin Carnival takes over Fort Kochi, and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale of contemporary art runs over the winter in Biennale years.

local_transport.text: Fort Kochi and Mattancherry are best explored on foot or by bicycle. To cross between Ernakulam and the islands, use the ferries or the Kochi Water Metro, India's first. Taxis and auto-rickshaws cover the rest.

where_to_stay.text: Fort Kochi, with its heritage homestays and small hotels, puts you among the sights and the cafes. Ernakulam on the mainland is more convenient for the station and has more large hotels, but you'll need a ferry or taxi to reach the old town.

overview.text:
Fort Kochi is the old heart of Kochi, shaped by Portuguese, Dutch and British rule. Its symbol is the row of Chinese fishing nets on the shore — huge cantilevered nets believed to have been introduced by Chinese traders. Watch them being raised in the late afternoon, then stay for sunset.

Behind the shore lie colonial streets full of art galleries and cafes. St Francis Church, first built in 1503, is one of the oldest European churches in India; Vasco da Gama died in Kochi in 1524 and was first buried here, before his remains were moved to Lisbon. The Santa Cruz Basilica nearby is known for its stained glass and painted interior. In the evening, catch a Kathakali performance at the Kerala Kathakali Center.

overview.text:
Mattancherry, just east of Fort Kochi, was once a busy centre of the spice trade, and many communities — Jews, Konkanis, Gujaratis and others — settled here. Its two great sights are side by side.

Mattancherry Palace, popularly called the Dutch Palace, holds fine Kerala murals of Hindu religious scenes along with portraits and possessions of the Rajas of Kochi. Next door, the Paradesi Synagogue was built in 1568 for the city's Paradesi Jewish community; it is closed on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and Jewish holidays. The lanes of Jew Town around it are lined with antique and spice shops.

overview.text:
Munnar — the name means 'three rivers' — sits where three mountain streams meet, about 1,600 m up in the Western Ghats. In the colonial era it was a summer retreat, and from the late 19th century its slopes were planted with tea; today the estates roll away in every direction.

The Tata Tea Museum at Nallathanni Estate tells the plantation story and ends with a tasting. Beyond the tea, Munnar has lakes such as Mattupetty and Kundala for boating, and Eravikulam National Park, home of the Nilgiri tahr, just outside town. Anamudi, the highest peak in South India at 2,695 m, rises nearby. Every twelve years the hills turn blue when the Neelakurinji shrub flowers.

Munnar is about 119 km from Cochin International Airport.

best_time.text: December to February is cool and pleasant. The monsoon, from June to September, brings heavy rain — lush, but with mist and slow mountain roads.

how_to_reach.text: The nearest airport is Cochin International, about 119 km away, and the nearest railhead is Ernakulam Junction, about 120 km. From there, the drive up into the hills takes several hours; buses run from most major towns in Kerala.

overview.text:
Eravikulam, established in 1978, was Kerala's first national park. It was created to protect the endangered Nilgiri tahr, a mountain goat, and today shelters the largest population of the species. Lion-tailed macaques and Nilgiri langurs also live here.

Most of the park is closed to the public; visitors can only enter the tourism zone at Rajamala, on the road from Munnar. Private vehicles aren't allowed inside, so you continue by the park's own transport and on foot. The views take in Anamudi, South India's highest peak, and once every twelve years the slopes turn blue with Neelakurinji flowers.

items.title: Opening hours

places.summary: The backwater capital of Kerala: houseboats on lakes and canals, the Nehru Trophy snake-boat race, beaches and Ayurveda.

overview.text:
Alappuzha — Alleppey — sits about 62 km south of Kochi and is the gateway to Kerala's most famous backwaters. Lord Curzon called it the 'Venice of the East'. The waterways here link five lakes and 38 rivers, threading past paddy fields, villages and coconut palms.

The classic way to see them is from a houseboat. These wooden boats once carried rice and spices; now they are floating rooms with bedrooms, bathrooms and a deck, and an overnight cruise is one of Kerala's defining experiences. On land, Alappuzha has a beach with a pier over 137 years old and a lighthouse, Ayurvedic centres, and the Ambalappuzha Sri Krishna Temple, famous for its sweet palpayasam. On the second Saturday of August, the Nehru Trophy Boat Race brings snake boats with crews of rowers to Punnamada Lake.

best_time.text: October to February is the ideal time to visit Alappuzha. Come in August for the Nehru Trophy Boat Race, held on the second Saturday of the month.

overview.text:
Thiruvananthapuram, or Trivandrum, is Kerala's capital. Its name means 'City of Lord Anantha', after the Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, whose mix of Kerala and Dravidian architecture and hidden treasure vaults make it the city's centre. In the 18th century Marthanda Varma founded the kingdom of Travancore and made the city his capital.

Travancore's legacy shows in the museum (opened 1857) and zoo, set in 55 acres in the middle of town, and in the Attukal Bhagavathy Temple, whose Pongala festival in February or March is noted as the largest gathering of women in the world. The Palayam Juma Masjid and St Joseph's Cathedral stand close together.

The city is the base for the south: Kovalam's beaches, Varkala's cliffs and Poovar's estuary on the coast, and Neyyar, Peppara and the hills of Ponmudi and Agasthyakoodam inland.

Kovalam is three crescent beaches side by side, about 16 km south of Thiruvananthapuram. A rocky headland shelters a bay of calm water for bathing, and the place has drawn visitors since the 1930s.

Lighthouse Beach, under the Vizhinjam lighthouse on Kurumkal hill, is the liveliest, lined with cafés; Hawah, or Eve's, Beach is a working fishing beach; Samudra, to the north, is quieter. Days are for swimming, Ayurvedic massages and catamaran rides, and the beach stays busy well into the night. Stays run from five-star hotels to budget cottages and Ayurvedic resorts.

Varkala, about 50 km north of Thiruvananthapuram, stands on sea cliffs — a rarity on Kerala's flat coast, and a National Geological Monument of the Geological Survey of India. Below them is Papanasam beach, named for a spring believed to wash away sins.

It is also a pilgrim town. The 2,000-year-old Janardhana Swamy Temple on the cliff is called the 'Varanasi of the South', and Sivagiri Mutt holds the samadhi of the reformer Sree Narayana Guru. Kerala Tourism notes that Varkala keeps a calm atmosphere, without Kovalam's bustle. There are jet skis, parasailing and surfing, with surf lessons at Kappil, where sea, river and backwater meet.

overview.text:
Kollam, one of the oldest ports on the Malabar Coast, grew rich on the spice trade. Today it is the centre of Kerala's cashew industry and the gateway to the backwaters: Ashtamudi Lake, named for its eight arms, is ringed by coconut groves and fishing villages, and the houseboat cruise from Kollam to Alappuzha is one of the most scenic in the state.

Kollam Beach is near the centre, with Thirumullavaram and Thangassery, and its old lighthouse, close by; Kollam Pooram fills Asramam Maidan. Inland are Jatayu Earth's Center at Chadayamangalam, with the world's largest bird sculpture, Thenmala — India's first planned eco-tourism destination — and the 300-ft Palaruvi waterfall.

overview.text:
Kumarakom is a village on the eastern shore of Vembanad, Kerala's largest lake, 14 km west of Kottayam. The classic trip is a houseboat across the lake to Alappuzha; in the canals behind the shore there is canoeing and kayaking.

The 14-acre Kumarakom Bird Sanctuary is at its best for resident birds in June–August and for migrants in November–February. The wider Vembanad–Kol wetland is a Ramsar site, and Pathiramanal island, out in the lake, is reached only by boat. Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things is set in Aymanam, next door.

Temperatures stay between 22 and 34°C. November to March is the best time; during the south-west monsoon backwater cruising is not allowed. Kumarakom is known for its fish and crab and its Ayurvedic resorts.

overview.text:
Thekkady lies at 900–1,800 m in Idukki district, on the Tamil Nadu border, and is the gateway to the Periyar Tiger Reserve — 777 sq km of forest, made a tiger reserve in 1978. More than 60 mammal and 265 bird species live here, but the forest is dense, so tiger sightings are highly unlikely; the boat on Periyar Lake is the best chance of elephants, bison and otters. The reserve can also be explored on treks and jeep safaris.

Kumily, 4 km away, is the busy town, with the bus station, spice traders and most budget stays; tea, cardamom, pepper and coffee estates surround the reserve. It drops to about 13°C in December–January and reaches 30°C in April–May; September to March is the best time.

Vagamon is a hill station at 1,100 m on the border of Kottayam and Idukki, 64 km from Kottayam and 25 km east of Erattupetta — tea gardens, meadows and a cool climate, with summer days of about 10–23°C. It became known only in 1926, when Walter Duncan and Company planted tea here.

Visitors come for hikes to waterfalls, rock climbing and paragliding, and for the glass bridge, India's longest cantilever glass bridge. Ilaveezhapoonchira, a treeless valley near Melukavu, 60 km from Kottayam, is known for its sunrises and sunsets.

overview.text:
Wayanad is a highland district in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, where Robusta coffee grows under forest shade at 700–2,100 m. Its best-known sights are the Edakkal Caves — a rock shelter, not truly a cave, with carvings discovered in 1895 — and Banasura Sagar, India's largest earthen dam, where boats go out on the reservoir.

Chembra Peak (2,100 m), the highest in the Wayanad hills, is climbed from Meppadi with forest-department guides, past a heart-shaped lake. Guided jeep safaris run in the Muthanga and Tholpetty ranges of the wildlife sanctuary, and there are waterfalls such as Soochippara, the Lakkidi viewpoint and the Thirunelli temple.

October to May is the best time. In the monsoon some areas may be closed after heavy rain.

overview.text:
Thrissur, the cultural capital of Kerala, is built around Thekkinkadu Maidanam, the hill that holds the Vadakkumnathan temple, and is home to the state's academies of music and drama, fine arts and literature.

Its great event is Thrissur Pooram in April or May, created by Sakthan Thampuran and now the largest pooram in India, with caparisoned elephants and massed drums. His palace, rebuilt in Kerala-Dutch style in 1795, is now a museum. The Basilica of Our Lady of Dolours is the city's great church.

Guruvayur, with one of South India's most revered Krishna temples, is nearby; Punnathur Kotta, 2 km from the temple, houses its elephants. Athirappilly falls are 59 km away.

overview.text:
Athirappilly is Kerala's largest waterfall: the Chalakudy River, coming down from the Western Ghats at the entrance to the Sholayar ranges, pours about 80 ft over rocks in three separate plumes. Vazhachal Falls is a short drive further up the road, and the forests around hold elephants, leopards, gaur, sambar and lion-tailed macaques.

The road is a forest highway towards Tamil Nadu, so night travel is not allowed — the checkpoints at either end close by 6:30 pm and all vehicles must be out by then. Plan it as a day trip from Thrissur, Kochi or Chalakudy.

overview.text:
Kozhikode, or Calicut, was one of the great ports of the medieval world, and Kappad beach marks where Vasco da Gama landed. Mananchira Square, once part of the Zamorins' palace, is now a park in the city centre.

It is Malabar's food capital: biryani, pathiri, seafood and the famous halwa, found along SM Street, the 'sweet street', and kallummakaya mussels at the beach, where people gather for sunsets by the old lighthouse and piers.

Beypore has a 1,500-year boatbuilding tradition and hosts an international water festival; Kadalundi bird sanctuary has mangroves and migrants. Vadakara's Lokanarkavu temple is tied to Kalaripayattu, and the hills hold the Thusharagiri and Arippara waterfalls. Kozhikode is also the gateway to Wayanad.

overview.text:
Kannur, about 280 km north of Kochi, is the cultural heart of North Malabar and best known for Theyyam, the ritual art in which performers become deities; the season runs from December to March.

The coast is uncrowded. Muzhappilangad, beside NH 66 towards Thalassery, is India's longest drive-in beach, about 4 km; Payyambalam is a quiet sunset beach near the station. St Angelo's Fort was built in 1505 by Francisco de Almeida, the first Portuguese viceroy. The Parassinikkadavu Muthappan Temple, on the Valapattanam River, is known for its open rituals and the dogs in its grounds.

Thalassery, nearby, gave its name to a biryani made with jeerakasala rice, and Kannur is Kerala's largest handloom district. October to March is the best time.

overview.text:
Bekal Fort, completed by Shivappa Nayaka of Keladi in 1650, is the largest fort in Kerala — about 40 acres of laterite on a headland, almost three-quarters of it washed by the sea. Tipu Sultan's observation tower gives views along the coast, and Bekal Beach lies right beside the walls.

Around it are the Valiyaparamba backwaters, cruised by houseboat; Chandragiri Fort at the mouth of the Payaswini; the Ananthapura lake temple near Kumbala; and the small hill station of Ranipuram at 780 m. Theyyam is performed in shrines and ancestral homes, and the 10-day Bekal International Beach Festival is held here. November to February has the best weather.

overview.text:
Marari Beach is the beach of Mararikulam, a village about 11 km from Alappuzha town, and many travellers use it as a quieter alternative to Alappuzha's own beach. It pairs well with the backwaters: stay a night or two by the sea before or after a houseboat on the Alappuzha canals.

Mararikulam has its own railway station, NH 66 passes 5 km to the east, and Cochin is the nearest airport. As for Alappuzha, October to February is the best time to come.

overview.text:
Poovar lies almost at the southern tip of Kerala, close to the harbour at Vizhinjam, where the Neyyar River runs into the Arabian Sea. Its estuary, where river, sea and backwater meet, is the reason to come: boat trips go out through the channels to the mangrove islands.

Poovar was once a trading port for timber, sandalwood, ivory and spices. Its name, 'flower river', is credited to Marthanda Varma of Travancore, who is said to have seen the Neyyar strewn with blossoms. It makes an easy half-day from Kovalam or Thiruvananthapuram.

overview.text:
Nelliyampathy is a hill village in Palakkad district, rising from 467 to 1,572 m, 60–65 km from Palakkad via Nemmara. The road enters past the 19th-century Pothundi dam and climbs to tea, cardamom and coffee estates and an orange farm.

The viewpoints are the draw — Seetharkundu, Manpara and Kesavanpara — with Victoria Church hills and the Karappara dam. Treks such as the 6-km walk to the hilltop need Forest Division permission. Further on, the Parambikulam sanctuary (285 sq km) has the giant Kannimara teak, and its tree house must be booked ahead.

Visit the estates and the orange farm.
